data.body:
Second controlled restart, and two data points now bound the growth rate. **The leak is faster than my first estimate, and the shape suggests it is driven by work done rather than time elapsed.**

**Restart 2, 2026-09-05 13:31 UTC** (triggered at my own 85% threshold, not by an incident):

    BEFORE   Mem: total 7813  used 6385  free 289   available 1223
             rebar-mcp-59d504c2bdbb-8093   3.563GiB / 7.631GiB
    AFTER    Mem: total 7813  used 3828  free 1492  available 3781
             rebar-mcp-59d504c2bdbb-8093 | Up 25 seconds (health: starting)
             curl localhost:8093/ -> 404      curl localhost:8080/ -> 200

Reclaimed ~2.5 GB. Same method as before: `docker restart` on the running container so it keeps its
name and nginx's upstream include stays valid.

**The two rates:**

| window | start | end | elapsed | rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| container 1 (observed) | ~368 MB | 4.566 GiB | ~2 h | ~2.1 GB/h |
| container 2 (measured end to end) | 368 MB | 3.563 GiB | ~56 min | **~3.4 GB/h** |

The second window is the cleaner measurement: I saw both endpoints of it directly — 368.5 MiB right
after restart 1, and 3.563 GiB immediately before restart 2 — whereas the first window's start is
inferred from what a fresh process weighs.

**A hypothesis this suggests, explicitly NOT established.** The second window was busier: six Gerrit
changes under review, a repo-wide canary blocker being iterated on, and several agents pushing
patchsets, versus a quieter first window. If the allocation is per-request rather than per-unit-time,
the rate should track request volume, and 2.1 -> 3.4 GB/h across a quiet-to-busy transition is
consistent with that. But n=2, I did not measure request volume, and I am not going to dress a
plausible correlation up as a mechanism — this repo has cost me two retractions tonight for exactly
that. The discriminating measurement is MCP RSS against request count over the same interval.

**Why it matters which one it is.** If time-driven, a periodic restart is a legitimate stopgap and
the interval is calculable. If request-driven, a restart schedule is unreliable — a busy hour
outruns it — and the mitigation has to be a bound on the allocation itself, or a memory limit on the
container so the kernel kills only the MCP rather than letting `git` trigger a global OOM that picks
its victim by size. The 03:13 UTC kill recorded above is exactly that global-OOM shape: `git` asked,
nothing was free, and the kernel chose the biggest process.

**Operationally, for whoever picks this up:** two restarts in one hour is not a sustainable posture,
and I am doing it manually. There is no automatic guard — `mcp_mem_abort` and `mcp_retire_cap`
metrics exist, which suggests someone anticipated MCP memory needing management, so the mechanism may
be present and unconfigured rather than missing. Worth checking before building a new one.
